# Error Design

*LLM first draft · human-edited once · frozen*

## Errors are part of the surface

Every exception a method can throw is part of what a caller must know.
The happy path is written once; the error paths are re-written in every
caller, forever — and they are the least-tested code in most systems.
Count it in any codebase: pick a method, list what it throws, and count
the `catch` blocks that exist across the code because of it. That
number is the cost of the method's error design. This Module teaches
the move that drives it toward zero: **define errors out of
existence** — not by swallowing failures, but by shrinking the set of
conditions that count as failures at all.

## The four moves, in order of preference

1. **Define the error out of existence.** Redefine the operation so the
   edge case is normal behavior. Deleting a file that does not exist can
   mean "ensure the file is gone" — success either way. Reading past the
   end of a range can return the overlapping portion — possibly empty,
   never a throw. Ask of each `throw`: what would this method's contract
   be if this case were simply allowed?
2. **Mask the error inside the module.** Handle the condition where the
   knowledge to handle it lives — retry the transient fault inside the
   client class, not in every caller. The error still happens; it stops
   being the caller's problem. This is the error-design form of a deep
   module: complexity absorbed behind the Target Interface, not pushed
   through it.
3. **Aggregate the handling.** When errors must propagate, catch them in
   one place — one handler at the outermost edge that maps failures to
   responses — instead of scattering `try`/`catch` through every
   controller and service. Ten handlers doing the same thing are nine
   too many.
4. **Crash.** For conditions that indicate a bug — a violated invariant,
   corrupted state — the correct handling is often none. Fail loudly at
   the fault instead of limping on to fail obscurely somewhere else.

## What this looks like in backend .NET

- **Exceptions are for the exceptional.** When a caller is expected to
  branch on an outcome — "not found", "already taken", "out of stock" —
  that outcome belongs in the return type (a bool, a Try-method, a
  result object), where the compiler makes the caller confront it. A
  `catch` used as an if-statement is control flow in a costume.
- **The thrown set is a design decision.** A method that lets
  `SqlException`, `HttpRequestException`, and `JsonException` escape has
  a contract that names three infrastructure technologies; callers now
  depend on your implementation choices. Mask those errors, or translate
  them into one type that speaks the caller's language.
- **Special values are errors in disguise.** Returning `null` where the
  caller will immediately dereference, or `-1` where the caller will
  index, moves the crash away from its cause without removing it.
  Defining the error out of existence means the returned value is
  usable as-is: an empty collection you can iterate, a no-op you can
  ignore.
- **Not every failure can be designed away.** The database will go
  down. Expected outcomes go in the return type; genuine failures
  propagate to one aggregated handler; impossible states crash. What
  must not survive is the middle mush: routine conditions thrown as
  exceptions and caught piecemeal at every call site.

## Three checks that need no taste

1. **The escape count.** For each public method, count the distinct
   exception types it can let escape. Every type above zero is a
   catalog entry every caller inherits.
2. **The happy-path catch.** Find every `catch` the code relies on to
   produce a normal outcome. Each one is an expected result miscast as
   an exception — the costume check above, run mechanically.
3. **The unless test.** Write each method's contract in one sentence,
   error cases included. A sentence that needs "unless" or "except"
   more than once is pointing at a restatement that would define the
   error out of existence — and the restatement usually is the
   redesign.

## How this runs in your Exercises

- In the refactor-type Exercise the Target Interface already defines
  every expected condition as an ordinary result — but the code behind
  it raises and catches its own exceptions for those same conditions,
  in every method. The Test Suite starts green; your job is to remove
  the exception traffic without changing a single answer.
- In the construct-type Exercise the temptation is the standard-library
  habit: throw on empty, throw on missing. The Target Interface's
  contract has already defined those cases out of existence — implement
  it so that no input the Test Suite can produce ever reaches a
  `throw`.
- Either way, finish with the three checks above. The Behavioral
  Checklist asks you the same countable questions, and they are the
  same questions to ask of every API you and an AI design together from
  now on.

modelExamples.caption: Defining the error out of existence: "delete an existing item" became "ensure the item is absent", so an absent item stopped being an error — it is the goal, already met. The before side confesses as much: its catch block's own comment says the "error" was exactly what the caller wanted. Redefine the contract and the handling code disappears from every caller at once.

An expected outcome moved out of the exception channel and into the return type. "Out of stock" is a branch every caller takes on an ordinary day, so throwing it forced each of them to write the everyday path in a catch block — control flow in a costume. As TryReserve's bool, the compiler puts the branch where the caller can see it; count the catch blocks a caller needs: one before, zero after.

Masking inside the module: the transient fault is handled by the one class that knows it is transient, instead of escaping to callers who each invent a retry policy — or forget to. The fault still occurs; what changed is who must know about it. Before: every caller carries error knowledge and a private copy of the loop. After: zero — the error-design form of a deep module.

exercises.title: Take the exceptions out of a seat map's everyday flow
exercises.smell: Exceptions used for expected control flow: the cinema seat map answers correctly and the boundary Test Suite starts green, but behind the Target Interface every expected outcome — unknown seat, seat already reserved, customer at the reservation limit — is raised as a custom exception by private helpers and caught again by the public methods, which translate each one back into false. The happy path runs on catch blocks, the same try/catch handling is duplicated in every method, and the internal exception catalog exists only to be swallowed. Refactor behind the Target Interface until the expected cases are ordinary conditionals and throw/catch disappear from src/, Test Suite green after every step.

exercises.title: Build a play queue with no errors left to handle
exercises.smell: The construct temptation is the standard library's own habit of throwing on the expected: Queue.Dequeue throws on empty, a Dictionary indexer throws on missing, and an implementer following those instincts turns every edge into an exception plus a catch block in some caller. This Target Interface has already defined those cases out of existence — playing from an empty queue returns silence, dropping a track that was never queued is a successful no-op, queuing a waiting track again moves it instead of failing. Implement it so that no input the Test Suite can produce ever reaches a throw: callers need zero catch blocks and know zero exception types.

checklistQuestions.prompt: Grep your finished src/ for throw and catch. Outside the Target Interface file, is the hit count zero?

options.label: Yes — no throw or catch survived

checklistQuestions.prompt: For each Target Interface member, count what a caller must do besides read the return value: exception types to catch, checks to make before calling, error state to inspect afterward. Is the total zero?

options.label: Yes — the return value is the whole contract
No — at least one extra obligation remains

checklistQuestions.prompt: Call every member in its former error case — play from an empty queue, drop what was never queued, release an unknown seat — and count the calls that threw. Is the count zero?

options.label: Yes — every edge came back as an ordinary answer
No — at least one call threw
